recent_posts.title: Schneier on Security
recent_posts.summary: Polymarket, a platform for betting on real-world events, is facing multiple integrity problems. Gamblers have threatened a journalist whose reporting was being used to verify a bet outcome, and someone allegedly used a hair dryer on weather sensors to manipulate weather-related bets. Additionally, insider trading on the platform appears to be widespread, raising serious questions about the viability and ethics of prediction markets.

recent_posts.title: Schneier on Security
recent_posts.summary: A ransomware negotiator pleaded guilty to secretly acting as a double agent, working for a ransomware gang while simultaneously negotiating ransom payments on behalf of victims. The case highlights a significant conflict of interest and trust betrayal in the cybersecurity incident response industry.

recent_posts.title: Schneier on Security
recent_posts.summary: Researchers have reverse-engineered Fast16, a piece of malware believed to be US state-sponsored and deployed against Iran years before Stuxnet. Fast16 spread across networks and silently manipulated computation in software performing high-precision mathematical calculations and physical simulations, causing failures ranging from faulty research results to catastrophic damage to real-world equipment — making it one of the most subtle sabotage tools ever observed in the wild.

recent_posts.title: Schneier on Security
recent_posts.summary: Mozilla's Firefox team, in collaboration with Anthropic, used an early version of Claude Mythos Preview to scan Firefox for security vulnerabilities. The result: 271 zero-days identified and fixed in Firefox 150, following an earlier scan with Opus 4.6 that found 22 bugs in Firefox 148. Security expert Bruce Schneier highlights this as an extraordinary milestone, noting that AI-powered vulnerability discovery at this scale could decisively shift the advantage to defenders — provided patches reach users quickly.

recent_posts.title: Schneier on Security
recent_posts.summary: Anthropic's Claude Mythos Preview can autonomously find and weaponize software vulnerabilities in critical infrastructure without expert guidance. Bruce Schneier and Barath Raghavan argue this is a real but incremental step in AI's growing role in cybersecurity. They propose a taxonomy separating patchable from unpatchable systems and easy-to-verify from hard-to-verify vulnerabilities, arguing defense will eventually benefit — especially for phones, browsers, and major services. Legacy IoT, industrial, and embedded systems remain at high risk. The authors advocate for VulnOps pipelines using defensive AI agents, continuous testing, documentation, and least-privilege principles as the new security baseline.

recent_posts.title: Schneier on Security
recent_posts.summary: A medieval encrypted letter sent by a Spanish diplomat has been fully decoded. The letter was rediscovered in 1860 and researchers have been working to decipher it ever since, with the decoding now complete.

recent_posts.title: Schneier on Security
recent_posts.summary: Bruce Schneier's recurring Friday Squid Blogging post shares science news about how squid and cuttlefish survived mass extinction events by retreating to oxygen-rich deep-sea refuges, based on newly sequenced genome analysis. The post also serves as an open thread for readers to discuss security news not covered elsewhere on the blog.

recent_posts.title: Schneier on Security
recent_posts.summary: A Dutch journalist demonstrated a significant security vulnerability by hiding a €5 Bluetooth tracker inside a postcard mailed to a Dutch naval warship. The tracker successfully revealed the ship's location for approximately 24 hours as it sailed in the Mediterranean, potentially exposing an entire carrier strike group. The incident revealed a gap in mail screening procedures — postcards, unlike packages, were not x-rayed before being brought aboard. Dutch authorities have since banned electronic greeting cards from being sent to naval vessels.

recent_posts.title: Schneier on Security
recent_posts.summary: The FBI forensically extracted deleted Signal messages from an iPhone by accessing the device's push notification database. Even after the Signal app was deleted, message content persisted in the internal notification store because the app was configured to show message previews on the lock screen. Signal has a setting to block message content from push notifications, and this case underscores why privacy-conscious users should enable it.

recent_posts.title: Schneier on Security
recent_posts.summary: ICE has publicly admitted to using spyware developed by the Israeli company Graphite, raising concerns about government surveillance and privacy.

top_posts.title: Schneier on Security
top_posts.summary: Leaked documents reveal that China's surveillance and propaganda infrastructure, including the Great Firewall, operates similarly to Western counterparts through private companies collaborating with academic institutions and competing for government contracts. The key difference is China's lack of transparency, with these operations only becoming visible through document leaks. The reality shows a market-driven approach rather than a centralized master plan, where censorship and propaganda tools are developed, marketed, and maintained like commercial products.

top_posts.title: Schneier on Security
top_posts.summary: LinkedIn job scams vary significantly across different countries, exploiting local economic conditions and employment patterns. In India, scammers target tech workers with fake high-paying roles. Kenya sees fake personal referrals due to an unorganized recruitment industry. Mexico's scammers advertise fraudulent formal positions to exploit the informal job economy. Nigeria's scams often trick users into sharing login credentials by promising paid work during high unemployment. These scams typically involve fraudulent employers requesting money for various fees, distinct from scams where fraudulent employees seek remote positions.

top_posts.title: Schneier on Security
top_posts.summary: Cryptocurrency ATMs have become a major vector for financial scams, charging excessive fees while enabling fraudsters to direct victims to purchase crypto on their behalf. The operators of these ATMs prioritize profits over consumer protection, showing little concern for the harm caused to victims.
